chapter.title: The bell that starts the line

cards.body: Your office coffee machine has a timer, a grinder and a spout, and that is every automation you have ever used: a start, some steps, a result. In n8n the start is a *trigger*, and in our picture it is **the bell on the assembly line**. No bell, no belt moves, no matter how many stations you have built.
cards.simpler: Think of the coffee machine at work. It has a timer, a grinder and a spout. That is every automation you have ever used: a start, a few steps, a result. In n8n the start is called a trigger. In our picture it is **the bell on the assembly line**. If the bell never rings, the belt never moves, no matter how many stations you have built along it.

cards.prompt: Priya builds a lovely 4-station line that reads a form, tidies the answers and emails her boss. She saves it, goes home, and it never runs. What is missing?

options.text: A faster belt. The stations are too slow to finish.
A bell. Nothing told the line to start.
A fifth station at the end that says 'done'.

whyNot.a: That's speed, not starting: a slow line still runs, but hers never began.
whyNot.c: That's the end of the line, not the beginning: it never reached the end because nothing woke it.

cards.reteach: Think of the bell as the only thing that can wake the line. Stations do their jobs only after the bell rings. In n8n that bell is the trigger, always the first box.

cards.title: Three parts, one bell
cards.body:
Every automation has three parts: a *trigger*, the one event that starts it; *actions*, the jobs it does; and a result you can see. n8n draws them as boxes on a canvas, joined left to right.

The trigger is always the first box, and it is **the only box that can wake the workflow**. You'd think a workflow runs when you save it. It doesn't. It sits like a shop with the lights off until its one event happens.

Three bells cover most jobs: a clock, a form being sent, or another app sending a signal. Tonight you use the clock, the *Schedule Trigger*, because it needs nothing but n8n.
cards.simpler: Every automation has three parts. A trigger is the one event that starts it. Actions are the jobs it does. Then there is a result you can see. n8n shows them as boxes on a canvas, joined left to right. The trigger is always the first box, and it is **the only box that can wake the workflow**. Saving a workflow does not run it. It waits, like a shop with the lights off, until its one event happens. Three triggers cover most jobs: a clock, a form being sent, or another app sending a signal. Tonight you use the clock, called the Schedule Trigger, because it needs nothing but n8n.

cards.title: Marco and the 8:00 count
cards.body: Marco runs online orders for a small bakery. Every morning at 8:00 he opened the orders sheet, counted the rows, and typed the number into the team chat. In n8n he adds a Schedule Trigger, sets it to 8:00 daily, and connects one node that sends him the message 'line started'. He clicks *Execute workflow* and 3 seconds later his phone buzzes: not at 8:00, but now, because **a hand-run skips the clock**. The clock only takes over once the line is switched on, and that switch is day 7.
cards.simpler: Marco handles online orders for a small bakery. Every morning at 8:00 he opened the orders sheet, counted the rows, and typed the number into the team chat. In n8n he adds a Schedule Trigger, sets it to 8:00 daily, and connects one node that sends him the message 'line started'. He clicks Execute workflow. Three seconds later his phone buzzes. Not at 8:00, but right now, because **a hand-run skips the clock**. The clock only takes over once the line is switched on. That switch is day 7.

cards.prompt: Dana wants a message in her team chat every Friday at 16:00 saying 'send the weekly report'. Which bell does she pick?

options.text: A form trigger, so the bell rings when someone fills in a form.
No trigger. She clicks Execute workflow herself each Friday.

whyNot.b: That's the form bell, not the clock: it rings when a person submits something, and nobody is submitting anything on Friday at 16:00.
whyNot.c: That's ringing the bell by hand, not automation: if she has to remember to click, she might as well remember to send the report.

cards.reteach: Match the bell to the event. 'Every Friday at 16:00' is a time, and time is the clock's job. The Schedule Trigger is the clock.

cards.title: Ringing it by hand
cards.body:
While you build, you ring the bell yourself. The *Execute workflow* button at the bottom of the canvas runs the line once, right now, ignoring the clock. It's how you check the stations before you trust them.

The clock only rings on its own when the workflow is switched on with the *Active* toggle, top right. Tonight, **leave Active off**. A line you are still poking at should not go off at 8:00 by itself.

Setup is short: n8n Cloud has a free trial, or install n8n on your own computer. Either way you land on a blank canvas with one button, Add first step, and that step is always a trigger.
cards.simpler: While you build, you ring the bell yourself. The Execute workflow button at the bottom of the canvas runs the line once, right now, and ignores the clock. That is how you check each station before you trust it. The clock only rings on its own when the workflow is switched on with the Active toggle, top right. Tonight, **leave Active off**. A line you are still poking at should not go off at 8:00 by itself. Setup is short. n8n Cloud has a free trial, or you can install n8n on your own computer. Either way you land on a blank canvas with one button, Add first step. That step is always a trigger.

cards.body: Sam sets a Schedule Trigger for 9:00, clicks Execute workflow at 9:00 sharp, watches it run, and tells the team it's live. Next morning: silence. The hand-run worked, but **nobody switched the clock on**. Spot it in 2 seconds: if the Active toggle top right is grey, the bell only rings when you press it.
cards.simpler: Sam sets a Schedule Trigger for 9:00, clicks Execute workflow at 9:00 sharp, watches it run, and tells the team it is live. Next morning, nothing happens. The hand-run worked, but **nobody switched the clock on**. You can spot this in two seconds. If the Active toggle in the top right is grey, the bell only rings when you press it yourself.

cards.prompt: A colleague says: 'I added a Slack node and a Google Sheets node, so my workflow has two bells now.' What do you tell them?

options.text: Right. Every node rings the bell once it's connected.
Those are stations, not bells. The bell is the first box, and neither of those is it.
Bells only come with the paid plan, so there are none yet.

whyNot.a: That's a station mistaken for the bell: Slack and Sheets nodes do jobs after the line starts; they don't start it.
whyNot.c: That's a guess about pricing, not about triggers: every copy of n8n has trigger nodes, free or paid.

cards.reteach: Count from the left. The first box is the bell, the trigger. Everything after it is a station waiting for the bell. Slack and Sheets are stations.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Every n8n workflow is a bell plus stations: the *trigger* is the only thing that wakes it, and the Schedule Trigger is a bell on a clock. While you build, you ring it yourself with Execute workflow, and **the clock only takes over once you switch the line on**.

Tomorrow: what actually travels down the belt, and why it is never just 'the data'.
cards.simpler: Every n8n workflow is a bell plus stations. The trigger is the only thing that wakes it up, and the Schedule Trigger is a bell on a clock. While you build, you ring the bell yourself with the Execute workflow button. Then **the clock only takes over once you switch the line on**. Tomorrow we look at what actually travels down the belt, and why it is never just 'the data'.

cards.body: Open n8n, click Add first step, pick Schedule Trigger, keep the default. Add an Edit Fields node after it with one field, greeting, set to hello. Click Execute workflow, then click Edit Fields and read its output on the right.
cards.simpler: Open n8n and click Add first step. Pick Schedule Trigger and keep the default setting. After it, add an Edit Fields node with one field. Name the field greeting and set its value to hello. Click Execute workflow. Then click the Edit Fields node and read its output on the right side of the screen. That output is **what your first line produced**.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now build a workflow that starts with a Schedule Trigger and run it by hand to watch it do one thing.
